inputs.description: Add a JSON output mode to the Product Anatomy runner (purpose/frameworks/product-anatomy/anatomy.mjs matrix --json): the substrate, and for each phase the flagship, ties, successor and every product's portfolio role, as one JSON document. Today the runner prints Markdown only, so its tests parse the table; the first handoff's lesson was that a parser read the wrong rows. Consumers: the runner's own test.mjs, run-handoff self-proofs, and agents that read the matrix. The Markdown output stays and is rendered from the same data. Node only, no dependencies, one file plus tests.
inputs.decision_question_answers:
M1 Source of truth. Which artifact should win when artifacts disagree, what form can it take (prose, structured data, executable tests, a formal contract or model, or running code), and who or what changes it?
  Answer: the role rules in code, checked by test.mjs; the JSON shape is stated in the README (tested)
M2 Knowability. Can correct behaviour be stated before building, or only discovered by building?
  Answer: knowable before building: the fields are those the Markdown already shows (tested)
M3 Requirements stability. How often will intent change, and is the change driven by learning or by outside rules?
  Answer: stable; the roles change only when Product Anatomy's rules change (assumed)
M4 Cost of being wrong and reversibility. What happens if it is built wrong, and how hard is it to undo?
  Answer: low; an internal tool, reversible in one commit (tested)
M5 Verifiability. How will we know it is correct: test, proof, inspection, measurement, use?
  Answer: high; tests compare JSON to the Markdown and to known fixtures (tested)
M6 Accountability. Must intent be provable later to a regulator, auditor, client or public?
  Answer: low; no outside party (tested)
M7 Builder. Who or what does the building, and what inputs can that builder reliably use?
  Answer: AI agents, gated by tests (tested)
M8 Lifespan. How long will this system live and be maintained?
  Answer: long enough to matter: every venture's matrix runs through it (assumed)
M9 Neighbours. What does it meet, which methodologies do those neighbours use, and what boundary contract is needed?
  Answer: one module; its boundary is the CLI and the JSON shape (tested)
M10 Switch conditions. What would make us change methodology?
  Answer: if other tools come to depend on the shape, treat it as a contract and version it (assumed)
M11 Evidence. Have we used this methodology on a similar system, and what happened?
  Answer: the previous handoff on the same file (anatomy-runner-fixes) ran as a small change with tests (tested)
M12 Time-to-market pressure. How strongly does the system need early user feedback and incremental shipping?
  Answer: low; nobody waits on it (tested)

fits_met.c: Requirements are stable enough to write a test specification for each level before building (unit, integration, system, acceptance)
A verification phase can be planned in parallel with each design stage, so every specification has a test that checks it
Behaviour must stay coherent across many sessions and readers
Core invariants that must never break

unfit_met.c: Types plus tests express the same thing more cheaply

fits_met.c: High reliability is needed and behaviour can be stated as automated tests (high verifiability)
Bugs, copy, styling, an obvious one-endpoint tweak

unfit_met.c: New module behaviour or a new public endpoint

fits_met.c: Any boundary between two systems or two agents
Several internal consumers whose needs diverge
Requirements are fixed and well understood before building starts (high knowability, low expected change)
A slice with known acceptance criteria, done in one agent session

unfit_met.c: Intent that must stay true for months

fits_met.c: The team can see its value stream end to end and has the authority to change how it works

unfit_met.c: A fixed, well-understood specification must be delivered exactly, so there is little waste to remove

fits_met.c: Work can be cut into fixed-length sprints that each produce something a user can see or use
The system is small or modular enough to build within a short timebox

unfit_met.c: Users cannot be available during development

fits_met.c: Prototypes or experiments can retire a risk before the next commitment is made

unfit_met.c: Small, low-risk work where the risk analysis costs more than it saves
Multiple consumers already depend on it

note: A recommendation only. The founder ratifies (I2).
